newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-NOBILO WINS WET GREENSBORO CLASSIC IN PLAYOFF OVER FAXON.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-NOBILO WINS WET GREENSBORO CLASSIC IN PLAYOFF OVER FAXON.

text.p: New Zealander Frank Nobilo, healthy again after mysterious wrist injuries, claimed the biggest win of his career by overtaking Brad Faxon in a playoff Sunday at the rainy Greater Greensboro Chrysler Classic.
Nobilo sank a par putt from seven feet at the first extra hole for victory after the pair had tied at 14-under-par 274 in a cold, steady rain on the waterlogged Forest Oaks course.

"Given the nature of what's happened the last six or seven months, this is probably the one I'm always going to remember," Nobilo said of his first U.S. PGA Tour victory, for which he received $342,000 and jumped to 17th on this year's money list.
Although technically a tour rookie, Nobilo is a hardened 36-year-old campaigner with five wins on the European Tour, where he has played most of his golf for the past decade.
But everything he has achieved in the past paled beside his magnficent finish Sunday as he came from six strokes behind Faxon over the final nine holes.
He made his move with four successive birdies starting at the 10th, then added another birdie at the 17th for a closing five-under 67, equal to the day's lowest round.
Faxon, playing behind, bogeyed the 17th to slip back into a tie, then parred the last for a 72.
The playoff began and ended at the par-four 18th, where Nobilo drove into the lush rough, from where he hacked a five-iron back to the fairway, before hitting a good lob wedge over the pin.

Faxon, meanwhile, reached the fringe with his second shot, but chipped eight feet past. His par putt missed to the right, which gave Nobilo, whose putt was on a similar line, no doubt about the break.
"I started mine inside left (edge of the cup) and closed my eyes," said Nobilo, whose winning putt curled into the centre of the hole.
"To come through this week, in this weather, on a course where every part of your game's tested, I think this (victory) will go to the top of the tree.

"That was as difficult conditions, weather wise, as I can remember playing in. It was very, very hard. You couldn't afford to hit a bad shot because when you hit it in the rough, it was very difficult to get it out."

Only last month, Nobilo pulled out of two successive tour events because of pain in his wrists and shoulders. But a visit to the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, just before the Masters reaped a rich reward.

He was prescribed a different medication, and since then he has been pain free. Even so, after missing the cut last week, he did not plan to play here until he was talked into it by fellow pro Ernie Els.

"When you haven't played well for a while, you really miss it," he said. "You wonder if it's ever going to come back and, if it does, when. Hopefully it'll give me more confidence to know that while it's tough here, on a good week I can win."
Nobilo said that although he would play mostly in the United States this year, he wanted to retain his European Tour membership.

"Ken Schofield (the European Tour executive director) said that if I play seven events, plus the majors, I can still be a member. That's something I'd like to try and do," said Nobilo, who will play the next two events on the PGA Tour before going back to Europe for the Volvo PGA Championship at Wentworth.
